newsitem.title: UK: Next UK government faces economic policy dilemma.
newsitem.headline: Next UK government faces economic policy dilemma.

text.p: Britain's next government will inherit an enviable combination of steady economic growth, falling unemployment and low inflation -- as well as an early policy dilemma over interest rates and taxes.
The last major economic statistics before the May 1 election, published on Wednesday, showed buoyant consumer demand, with retail sales rising 4.0 percent in March from a year earlier.
But the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said manufacturers were suffering from the exceptionally strong pound, which makes it more difficult to sell their goods abroad.

And Bank of England Governor Eddie George renewed his warning that interest rates need to rise to 6.25 percent from the present 6.0 percent to prevent underlying inflation -- now at historically low levels -- from heading higher again.

Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC Markets, says the retail sales figures and the CBI's industrial trends survey highlight the dilemma facing the next Chancellor of the Exchequer -- which opinion polls suggest is likely to be the opposition Labour party's Gordon Brown.
"Whilst the consumer sector needs action to prevent it from overheating, sharp rises in interest rates could push industry back into recession," Loynes said.
He and other economists in the City of London are increasingly arguing that the best course of action for a new government would be a fiscal tightening -- a euphemism for raising taxes.

"The obvious solution to this problem would be for a major tightening of fiscal policy, taking the steam out of domestic demand, reducing the need to raise rates and thereby softening sterling," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist James Barty wrote in a study entitled "Labour's Economic Inheritance."
The problem for a Labour government is that it has effectively tied its own hands on taxes.

As part of its efforts to assure British voters that it is no longer a party of high taxation, Labour has promised not to raise income tax rates and to live within extremely tight public spending constraints laid down by the Conservative government.
"This means that Mr Brown will have to rely on monetary policy to bring a slowdown in the economy and that brings with it the problem of sterling," Barty said.

John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, said most people in the financial markets believe interest rates will need to rise -- he expects a move to 6.50 percent in two quarter-point steps.
But he argues that the problems facing the next government should be kept in perspective.

"Whoever comes into power on May 2 will look at an economy which is overall in very good shape," he said. "We've got firm growth, unemployment declining sharply and an inflation rate which is by historical standards extremely low."

Shepperd believes the pound's strength owes much to the recent rally in the dollar, which now appears to be abating. The markets have already discounted higher British interest rates and the pound may therefore shrug off any increases, he said.

"Interest rate expectations may be scaled back during the year and that might take some of the heat out of sterling," Shepperd said. "If we have seen the peak in the dollar, which is our working assumption, then I don't think we're going to see any further appreciation in sterling on the back of an interest rate increase."
The Bank of England, which has pressed unsuccessfully for interest rate increases throughout this year, has acknowledged "the real dilemma which sterling's effective appreciation posed for policy."

But at his March 5 monetary meeting with Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke, Bank Governor Eddie George said strong consumer demand would put upward pressure on inflation unless urgent action was taken to curb it.
Minutes of the meeting, published on Wednesday, show George commenting that monetary policy-makers can do very little directly to affect the exchange rate.

"The Bank's concern was that, if, on account of the exchange rate, the necessary tightening of policy to moderate the pace of domestic expansion was delayed, then more substantial tightening would eventually become unavoidable," George said.
